title: End of Year Motivation Moves, Part 2 — Work the Roster
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: This piece is part 2 of Dave Stuart Jr.'s End of Year Motivation Moves mini-series and introduces "working the roster," the practice of deliberately having a brief moment of genuine connection (MGC) with every student on a class roster, each one built around a specific expression of thanks. Stuart argues the exercise is as much for the teacher's own heart as for student motivation, since it forces teachers to find something appreciative to say even about students they've had a hard time with all year. He walks through four worked examples of what these thank-you MGCs sound like in practice, showing that specific, personalized language about a student's traits, struggles, and growth is what makes the gesture land rather than feel generic. The underlying claim is that systematically working through an entire roster near year's end reshapes a teacher's own disposition toward students while also boosting perceived credibility.
points: "Work the roster" turns end-of-year relationship-building into a systematic practice: print every student's name and commit to a 30-60 second thank-you MGC with each one.

The exercise's real value lies in its difficulty with hard-to-reach students — being forced to find something genuinely appreciative to say about a challenging student reshapes the teacher's own perspective on them.
Stuart's four worked examples model how specificity, naming a student's traits, struggles, or growth over the year, is what makes a thank-you MGC feel authentic rather than generic praise.
The tactic doubles as self-care: Stuart frames it as something that changes how the teacher feels about the year, not just how students feel about the teacher.
quotes: It's hard in a good way — for students you've had a hard time with, you'll have to take some time or a walk just to try to figure out what to say to them about what you've appreciated.
You know, there was a time this year when this kind of drove me crazy about you. Funny, right? But look: I think it's something special about you, this mind that wants to know how things work.
You've wrestled, haven't you? You've fought! There've been lots of times when you've told yourself — don't deny it, you said it right in front of me! — "I can't do this. I'm going to fail.
Early in the school year, I don't think we quite knew what to make of each other. Or, let me just speak for me — I didn't know what to make of you!
The person I see in front of me today is a different, deeper, stronger person than the one I met last September. Thanks for letting me in on a bit of your life story, Herbert.
